chunks: "SPI is faster, and there are two reasons, one electrical and one protocol.
Electrically, SPI drivers are push-pull: the output transistors actively pull the line up and down, so edges take a few nanoseconds and the clock can run at 10 to 50 megahertz or more.
I2C is open-drain. A device can only pull the line low; to go high, a pull-up resistor has to charge the bus capacitance. That's an RC curve, with a rise time of about 0.
85 R pC b . With 4. 7 kilohms and 100 picofarads that's about 400 nanoseconds, which is already too slow for 400 kilohertz mode.
You can shrink the resistor, but then you burn current every time the line is low, and the spec caps how much current devices must sink, so I2C tops out around 1 megahertz in practice.
The second reason is overhead. SPI sends 8 clocks per byte. I2C sends 9, because of the ACK bit, plus an address byte and often a register-pointer byte and a repeated start.
So reading 14 bytes is about 380 microseconds on 400 kilohertz I2C versus 12 microseconds on a 10 megahertz SPI link, roughly 30 times faster.
The one caveat is that UART isn't clocked, so its speed is just baud rate, usually 115200 up to a few Mbaud."
